transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-04-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE backup), Priya Iyer (HollowGrove Network), Tom Brooks (CTO), Sara Alvarez (InfoSec), Jin Woo (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Customer evaluating private deployment / VPC-only access for sensitive analytics workloads.
- Primary concerns: CIDR overlap, egress IPs, transit gateway vs peering, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2 evidence and audit logs, region gating.
- Agreed next steps: share IP worksheet, schedule technical deep dive, start POC account.

Topics noticed: network topology, private endpoints, region constraints, latency vs cost tradeoffs, security/compliance, pilot timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Lena, AE for Redwood Inference, and with me is Marcus Chen our SE. Uh, thanks for taking the time, Tom, Priya, Sara. Can you quickly introduce?
[00:12] Tom Brooks: Yeah hi, Tom here, CTO at HollowGrove. We're evaluating options to run inference on private infrastructure, we want to avoid public egress, need strong auditability.
[00:20] Priya Iyer: Priya, I run the network side, I'll own CIDR planning and peering configs.
[00:26] Sara Alvarez: Sara from InfoSec, short on time but want to vet KMS, key management, and retention policies.
[00:31] Marcus Chen: Great. Quick agenda: basic architecture options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), network paths for private, peering/topology options, IP/egress planning, and security controls. Then we'll list next steps.
[00:43] Priya Iyer: Perfect. My main questions up front: can Redwood support private endpoints (privatelink style) into our VPCs, do you require transit gateway, and what about CIDR overlap detection?
[00:56] Marcus Chen: Yes, we have a private deployment option that uses customer VPC peering or privatelink-like endpoints depending on cloud provider. For AWS we support VPC peering and PrivateLink endpoints; for GCP it's VPC peering or private services connect, for Azure it's private endpoints. There are tradeoffs: peering is simpler but scales with peer count; TGW/transit is better for multi-VPC architectures.
[01:21] Tom Brooks: We run multi-account AWS with a transit gateway, we prefer to keep everything funneled through TGW and use egress NAT at a central egress stack. How would that look?
[01:32] Marcus Chen: You can route to Redwood's private endpoints via a centralized TGW attachment. In practice customers either attach Redwood subnets to their TGW or use cross-account privatelink. If you want TGW we recommend adding route entries to route traffic from your subnets to the Redwood attachment, then restrict via SGs and NACLs. There was a slight pause (voice): sometimes our docs call it a 'private onramp'.
[01:58] Priya Iyer: CIDR overlap is a deal stopper for us. Do you have reserved CIDR ranges or can we pick from your side?
[02:06] Marcus Chen: We provide a set of suggested IP ranges for the peering endpoints. For peering we do static IP ranges per deployment; for PrivateLink we expose ENIs in your account so overlap is less common but still possible at the VPC/subnet level. We'll run an overlap check during intake.
[02:25] Sara Alvarez: On the security side, we need KMS integration and we want to ensure keys never leave our account. Can Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS or HSM?
[02:33] Lena Park: Short answer: yes. For Private deployments our control plane can be configured to use your KMS for encryption at rest for model artifacts and logs. We'll share the KMS integration guide. One caveat is in hosted model variants we need to discuss key rotation workflows — Marcus can follow up.
[02:50] Marcus Chen: Right, for on-prem or VPC-deployed inference nodes you can mount a KMS or HSM and we support encrypting local volumes with CMKs. For hosted shared environments we have envelope encryption and can integrate with partner KMS solutions, but for strict key ownership you'd want Private.
[03:08] Tom Brooks: Latency is also a factor. Our application is latency sensitive (<80ms p95). How do private endpoints affect tail latency versus a directly hosted API?
[03:18] Marcus Chen: Private endpoints add network hops; when co-located in same region we typically see sub 10ms added in most cloud regions. The much larger latency contributors are model size and batch windows. If you need <80ms p95 we can profile with your traces and select smaller model variants or reserved dedicated capacity with guaranteed SLOs.
[03:39] Priya Iyer: Are there egress IPs from Redwood side we need to whitelist? We prefer a static egress set to lock down outbound flows.
[03:47] Marcus Chen: For Private deployments we can offer static egress IPs per deployment — those are the IPs used for outbound calls (updates, telemetry if enabled). For fully air-gapped setups, you can disable egress and rely on local model artifacts. We'll document the egress ranges.
[04:02] Sara Alvarez: Audit logs: do we get request-level logs for model inference? We need to correlate to our SIEM.
[04:09] Lena Park: Yes we emit audit logs and request-level metadata to a logging sink. For Private we can push to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Log Analytics via VPC peering or direct ingestion. We'll provide log schema and retention options.
[04:26] Jin Woo: Quick nit: what about KV cache and prefix caching, does that live on your side or in our VPC?
[04:33] Marcus Chen: KV cache for inference lives with the serving runtime. In Private deployments it runs inside your VPC so the cache nodes live in your network, reducing cross-account traffic. In hosted variants the cache is on Redwood infrastructure and we handle caching policies.
[04:48] (crosstalk)
[05:00] Tom Brooks: What about multi-region data residency: we have EU customers that must keep data in eu-west-1 only, can we gate model inference to that region?
[05:09] Marcus Chen: Yes, you can pin deployments to regions and we can set routing policies by customer or by model. For Private deployments we'd spin up nodes in eu-west-1 or an on-prem cluster. You can also enforce region gating in the control-plane config so traffic never leaves selected regions.
[05:28] Priya Iyer: For peering, do you prefer/require non-overlapping /24s or are /20s acceptable? Our VPCs use /16 in some accounts.
[05:37] Marcus Chen: We recommend /24 subnets for endpoint ENIs, but can work with larger ranges; it's about avoiding overlap and proper route table entries. If you use /16s we may need to coordinate more carefully—overlapping with a /16 could break routing.
[05:50] Lena Park: If helpful we have an IP planning worksheet that Marcus can share — has example CIDR allocations and a checklist.
[05:56] Priya Iyer: Yes please.
[05:58] Marcus Chen: I'll attach that after the call.
[06:02] Tom Brooks: On compliance — SOC2 plus we want to see pen test artifacts. Do you have SOC2 Type II?
[06:08] Lena Park: We do. We'll send the SOC2 summary and redacted Type II report under NDA, plus our recent penetration test summary. 
[06:17] Sara Alvarez: What about SSO and RBAC for the control plane? We need SAML + SCIM provisioning, and just-in-time provisioning for engineers.
[06:24] Lena Park: Redwood Console supports SAML SSO and SCIM, and RBAC with fine-grained project/route/model permissions. We'll include the SSO setup guide in the follow-up.
[06:33] Jin Woo: A corner case: we use a hub-and-spoke with shared services VPC — can Redwood live in the shared services VPC and be consumed by spokes without per-spoke peering?
[06:43] Marcus Chen: Yes, that's a common pattern. If your shared services VPC is attached to TGW and spokes route to it, Redwood can be deployed into the shared services VPC and spokes route through TGW. Be mindful of asymmetric routing and ensure return paths exist.
[07:02] Priya Iyer: Do you support provable isolation of logs and audit trails per tenant?
[07:09] Lena Park: For Private deployments you can keep logs in your account; for Dedicated we provide tenant-separated logging and for hosted we provide logical separation plus optional dedicated logging pipelines for enterprise.
[07:21] (brief silence)
[07:35] Tom Brooks: Our timeline: we want a pilot by mid-April and production gating by end of Q2. Is that feasible?
[07:44] Lena Park: That timeline sounds reasonable. Pilot + smoke test within 2 weeks, ramp to prod over 6-8 weeks depending on integration work.
[07:53] Priya Iyer: For the pilot, is it possible to do a handshake flow where we first let a small subset of subnets talk to a POC endpoint?
[07:59] Marcus Chen: Absolutely. We'll provision a POC deployment with limited CIDR and test keys. Typically customers start with a single AZ for the pilot.
[08:10] Tom Brooks: Any requirement for egress NAT to your side for updates? We're behind strict firewall rules.
[08:18] Marcus Chen: For updates and control plane telemetry we need outbound to Redwood's update endpoints. We can either allow specific egress IPs or set up a private peering that carries control plane traffic. For hardened setups we can also schedule manual bundle uploads.
[08:33] Sara Alvarez: Manual bundle uploads meaning we can ship model artifacts via S3 replication?
[08:39] Marcus Chen: Yes, or you can have us pull from a signed S3 URL over an egress path you permit.
[08:45] Priya Iyer: Ok. A practical question: how long does peering take during the intake—what's the brownfield window?
[08:52] Marcus Chen: From network side, if CIDRs are well-defined, peering set up is typically a few hours to a day; TGW attachments and policy setup can be 1-3 days depending on approvals. The longer part is CP/security review and any firewall exceptions.
[09:04] Lena Park: Let's do a quick walkthrough of the two architecture sketches (Lena references screen-share - rough description follows).
[09:12] Marcus Chen: Architecture A: Single-VPC private endpoints in your shared services VPC. Pros: simple, single peering. Cons: single point of failure if shared services goes down. Architecture B: Per-environment deployments with TGW attachments; Pros: isolation per environment, more control; Cons: more peering and route management.
[09:38] Tom Brooks: For A we worry about blast radius. B seems more operationally heavy. Which is typical for customers that need strict compliance?
[09:46] Marcus Chen: Many compliance-focused customers pick B because they can separate prod/stage via distinct VPCs and restrict cross-VPC routing. If you have TGW it's natural. If not, PrivateLink-based ENIs per VPC reduce blast radius as well.
[10:00] Priya Iyer: We also have to account for NAT IP reuse — our egress pool is small, will Redwood's static egress IPs map cleanly?
[10:08] Marcus Chen: We'll provide a list of egress IPs; if you need more than one NAT IP we can allocate a block. For high throughput we recommend using multiple IPs and proper SNAT mapping.
[10:20] (short back-and-forth about SNAT)
[10:35] Tom Brooks: What about load balancing—do you expect us to put an NLB in front of the endpoint ENIs?
[10:41] Marcus Chen: Typically not necessary — PrivateLink will provide ENIs and the cloud's NLB is used for cross-AZ balancing if you use a private service model. For peering-based setups the routing is handled by VPC route tables and SGs.
[10:58] Sara Alvarez: Data retention question: inference request logs — can we set retention to 90 days and auto-delete?
[11:05] Lena Park: Yes retention is configurable per customer; for Private you can also enforce retention policies in your own logging account.
[11:14] Priya Iyer: A gotcha—our VPCs use overlapping 10.0.0.0/16 ranges in different accounts for historical reasons. That will complicate peering.
[11:23] Marcus Chen: Right, overlapping /16 across accounts can block peering. For that we'd recommend PrivateLink or a shared services deployment in a non-overlapping VPC. We'll help map an approach.
[11:36] (sound of keyboard)
[11:44] Tom Brooks: Any support for on-prem connectors? We have an edge site for cache pre-processing.
[11:50] Marcus Chen: Yes we offer an on-prem package for air-gapped or hybrid; it runs as a self-hosted control plane and inference runtime. That tends to be heavier support and licensing but works for sensitive data.
[12:02] Lena Park: Let's capture concrete asks — Priya you'll share CIDRs and a diagram, Marcus will share IP worksheet and peering guide, Lena will send SOC2/pen test and pricing ballpark. Does that align?
[12:14] Priya Iyer: Yes.
[12:17] Tom Brooks: Yep.
[12:19] (pause)
[12:30] Marcus Chen: One more operational note: if you want guaranteed latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated reserved capacity in the region plus the private network path. That avoids noisy neighbor issues.
[12:42] Lena Park: Good callout. Ok last item — timeline and acceptance criteria. What would you need to sign off pilot?
[12:49] Tom Brooks: Pilot acceptance: successful end-to-end inference with sample traffic within region, no public egress, observed p95 latency under 120ms for our model, and audit logs delivered to our logging account.
[13:03] Sara Alvarez: And security review signoff — I need to see SOC2 artifacts and a short runbook for incident response.
[13:12] Lena Park: We'll include those in the package.
[13:16] (wrap-up chatter)
[13:25] Lena Park: Great — we'll follow up with the documents and schedule the deep-dive. Thanks everyone.

End transcript.
